subject: Longitudinal analysis with spatial power law covariance.

messages.author: 9572ba991834d61e
messages.subject: Longitudinal analysis with spatial power law covariance.
parts:
I'd like to be able to run an analysis similar to something I have run in SAS and R (as a jumping off point to make sure I have the Bayesian model right before I start changing things to get what I want out of Bayes), but I'm having trouble when I use real data, so I was wondering the best way to optimize the following model (this is within R):

library(nlme)
library(rstan)

set.seed(1234)

# Create data
df <- data.frame(id=factor(rep(1:10,each=9)),
                 day=factor(rep(1:9,times=10)),
                 dayn=rep(1:9,times=10),
                 group=factor(rep(1:2,each=45)),
                 resp=rnorm(90,1:9))

# I would like to pattern the Bayesian analysis off of this model
fit.spl <- gls(resp~day+group+day:group,
               data=df,
               corr=corCAR1(,form=~dayn|id))

# Extract the modle matrix
mm <- model.matrix(lm(resp~day*group, data=df))

# Create a matrix that represents the response values
ymat <- t(matrix(df$resp,ncol = 10))

# Force the model matrix into a three dimensional array
tda <- array(t(mm),dim=c(18,9,10))

# Create the data list
data_list <- list(N=nrow(ymat),
                  K=ncol(ymat),
                  J=nrow(tda),
                  y=ymat,
                  x=tda,
                  Day=1:9)

# The model code
model_code <- '
data {
  int N;
  int K;
  int J;
  vector[K] y[N];
  real x[J,K,N];
  vector[K] Day;
}
parameters {
  row_vector[J] beta;
  real<lower=0.0000001> sig; # Variance
  real rho; # Correlation
}
transformed parameters {
  cov_matrix[K] Sigma;  # The covariance matrix
  for(m in 1:K) Sigma[m,m] <- sig;  # Assign the diagonal elements
  for(m in 1:(K-1)) {
    for(n in (m+1):K) {
      Sigma[m,n] <- sig*rho^(Day[n]-Day[m]);  # Allows unequally spaced days
      Sigma[n,m] <- Sigma[m,n];  # Maintain symmetry
    }
  }
}
model {
  vector[K] mu[N];
  for (n in 1:N) {
    mu[n] <- to_vector(beta * to_matrix(x[,,n]));
    y[n] ~ multi_normal(mu[n], Sigma);
  }
}
'

fit0 <- stan(model_code = model_code,data = data_list,chains = 0)
fit1 <- stan(fit=fit0,data=data_list,warmup = 100, iter=200, seed=1111)

This actually does a pretty good job, and if I increased the sampling it would get really close.  But it doesn't run as fast as I would like it to, and when I use real data, the estimates end up with very high Rhat values and very low n_eff values.  What can I do to increase efficiency and numerical stability?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Longitudinal analysis with spatial power law covariance.
parts:
1. You don't need the lower=0.00001 thing --- just
use lower=0.

2. If rho really is a correlation, it needs <lower=-1, upper=1>.

3. Vectorize multi_normal. Instead of

> for (n in 1:N) {
> mu[n] <- to_vector(beta * to_matrix(x[,,n]));
> y[n] ~ multi_normal(mu[n], Sigma);
> }

where I'm assuming a new data variable xx declared as:

matrix[K, J] xx[N];

where your x was declared as

> real x[J,K,N];


and where xx is defined to be:

xx[n, k, j] = x[j, k, n]

You can either define xx in transformed data and just
do the loop to create it, or change the way you input data
to the progrma.

Then you can declare beta as a regular (column)
vector and use

mu[n] <- xx[n] * beta;

with mu declared as before, and then vectorize the multivariate normal:

y ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma);

This should be much much faster, especially if N >> 1.

- Bob
